      /* nock_port_open -- is something already listening on the loopback port? A non-blocking connect with
       * a 100 ms budget: no DNS, no blocking connect, no sleeping for a fixed time and hoping. */
      static int nock_port_open(int port) {
          struct sockaddr_in addr;
          memset(&addr, 0, sizeof addr);
          addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
          addr.sin_port = htons((unsigned short)port);
          addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_LOOPBACK);
      #ifdef _WIN32
          static int wsa_ready = 0;
          if (!wsa_ready) {
              WSADATA w;
              if (WSAStartup(MAKEWORD(2, 2), &w) == 0) wsa_ready = 1;
          }
          SOCKET s = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
          if (s == INVALID_SOCKET) return 0;
          u_long nonblocking = 1;
          ioctlsocket(s, FIONBIO, &nonblocking);
          int rc = connect(s, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof addr);
          if (rc != 0 && WSAGetLastError() != WSAEWOULDBLOCK) { closesocket(s); return 0; }
          fd_set wr;
          FD_ZERO(&wr);
          FD_SET(s, &wr);
          struct timeval tv;
          tv.tv_sec = 0;
          tv.tv_usec = 100000;
          rc = select(0, NULL, &wr, NULL, &tv);
          int ok = rc > 0;
          closesocket(s);
          return ok;
      #else
          int s = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
          if (s < 0) return 0;
          int flags = fcntl(s, F_GETFL, 0);
          fcntl(s, F_SETFL, flags | O_NONBLOCK);
          int rc = connect(s, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof addr);

That is what makes relaunching the client work:\n *    a server from a previous session is still running and still holds the world, so we ATTACH\n *    instead of spawning a second one that would fail to bind and die. It is also the honest way to\n *    answer \"is a world already up?\" without a lockfile that goes stale when a process is killed.\n *\n *  - Zone validation. The zone id becomes a real filename on both sides\n *    (var/maps/proc_<zone>.json, apps/server/src/main.c) and travels in PACKET_ZONE_STATE, so an id\n *    that can escape the map directory, or one that starts with '-' and would be read as a flag by\n *    the child, is rejected here at the entry point instead of failing later as a mystery.\n */\n#ifndef SHANKPIT_COOP_HOST_H\n#define SHANKPIT_COOP_HOST_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n#define COOP_HOST_DEFAULT_PORT 6969 /* the live queue port; MODE_QUEUE clients already default here */\n#define COOP_HOST_DEFAULT_ZONE \"dungeon_1\" /* apps/server/src/main.c's own --dungeon default */\n#define COOP_HOST_ZONE_MAX 32\n#define COOP_HOST_ARG_MAX 8\n\ntypedef struct {\n    char zone[COOP_HOST_ZONE_MAX];\n    int port;\n} CoopHostConfig;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    int ok;      /* 1 = a world is reachable on this port (spawned now, or already running) */\n    int attached; /* 1 = nothing was spawned; an existing server already owns the port */\n    long pid;    /* child pid (POSIX) when spawned; 0 when attached or on Windows */\n    char error[160]; /* why ok == 0, in words fit to put on screen */\n} CoopHostResult;\n\n/* Zone ids: 1..COOP_HOST_ZONE_MAX-1 chars of [A-Za-z0-9_-], and not starting with '-'.\n * The conservative set is on purpose -- the id is a filename component and a wire string. */\nint coop_host_zone_valid(const char *zone);\n\n/* Usable unprivileged ports only; anything else is a typo or an attempt to bind something real. */\nint coop_host_port_valid(int port);\n\n/* Fill `out` from optional arguments, applying the defaults above. Absent/empty zone and a\n * non-positive port take the default. Returns 1 on success; 0 (out untouched) if a supplied value is\n * invalid, so a bad argument is refused rather than silently replaced by a default. */\nint coop_host_config(CoopHostConfig *out, const char *zone, int port);\n\n/* Describe the child's command line: argv = { bin, \"--port\", port_buf, \"--dungeon\", zone, NULL }.\n * Separate from the spawn so the exact arguments are testable without starting a process. */\nint coop_host_fill_argv(const CoopHostConfig *cfg, char *argv[COOP_HOST_ARG_MAX], char port_buf[8]);\n\n/* Is another process bound to 0.0.0.0:<port> (UDP)? 1 = busy, 0 = free. A probe failure (no socket)\n * answers 0 -- \"free\" -- because spawning and letting the child report a bind error is a better\n * outcome than refusing to start a world at all. */\nint coop_host_port_busy(int port);\n\n/* Start `server_bin` with this config and confirm it did not die on startup. On POSIX the child is\n * forked and exec'd with coop_host_fill_argv's exact argv; on Windows CreateProcessA(CREATE_NO_WINDOW)\n * with the equivalent command line. The child is intentionally not waited on: a hosted world outlives\n * the lobby window, and the port probe above is what makes a relaunch rejoin it instead of racing it. */\nint coop_host_start(const char *server_bin, const CoopHostConfig *cfg, CoopHostResult *out);\n\n#endif /* SHANKPIT_COOP_HOST_H */\n"
}

si.cb = sizeof si;\n    ZeroMemory(&pi, sizeof pi);\n    if (!CreateProcessA(NULL, cmdline, NULL, NULL, FALSE, CREATE_NO_WINDOW, NULL, NULL, &si, &pi)) {\n        snprintf(out->error, sizeof       // app_launch_status -- real, honest, on-screen feedback (never silent) for lobby_launch_app
      // below; drawn next to the page-toggle button whenever non-empty.
      static char app_launch_status[160] = "";
      
      // lobby_app_binary_path -- real path search, documented rather than hand-waved: the intended
      // real distribution shape is `<dir the SHANKPIT binary itself runs from>/bundled/<name>`
      // (nothing populates that directory yet -- real, separate packaging/CI follow-up, not built in
      // this pass) with a fallback to this monorepo's own sibling-repo dev layout
      // (`../DEADWEIGHT/build/dw_gui`) so launching actually works today, in this repo's own real dev
      // environment, rather than only after a packaging step that doesn't exist yet. Returns 1 and
      // fills `out` on success, 0 (out untouched) if nothing was found at either location.
      static int lobby_app_binary_path(const char *bundled_name, const char *dev_relative_path, char *out, size_t out_sz) {
          char *base = SDL_GetBasePath();
          if (base) {
              char candidate[1024];
              snprintf(candidate, sizeof candidate, "%sbundled/%s", base, bundled_name);
              FILE *f = fopen(candidate, "rb");
              if (f) {
                  fclose(f);
                  snprintf(out, out_sz, "%s", candidate);
                  SDL_free(base);
                  return 1;
              }
              char dev_candidate[1024];
              snprintf(dev_candidate, sizeof dev_candidate, "%s%s", base, dev_relative_path);
              f = fopen(dev_candidate, "rb");
              if (f) {
                  fclose(f);
                  snprintf(out, out_sz, "%s", dev_candidate);
                  SDL_free(base);
                  return 1;
              }
              SDL_free(base);
          }
          return 0;
      }
      
      /* ---- local NOCK app: launch the map-tools server + open the editor page ---------------------
       * Until now the local NOCK map tools needed a separate `make local-nock` in another terminal (or a
       * Windows .bat) before the editor was reachable. As an APPS entry, NOCK is one click: it starts the
       * same server itself and opens http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ in the system browser, and the browser tab
       * plus the in-game EDIT MAP live session are the same room (levels save to levels/<name>.json and
       * are committed, exactly as `make local-nock` does).
       *

  content: |
      # Unifying GoblinFoxDragon with SHANKPIT — plan, and what phase 1 actually shipped
      
      The founder: *"we need to start unifying gfd and shankpit archipelligo ... shankpit is the frontend for the
      MMO ... GFD is a fork of SHANKPIT maybe its time to unfork it and just merge GFD all of it needs to be
      brought into shankpit and the shankpit engine improvements that are already in place dont get overwritten
      ... including bringing in the GFD exclusive levels ... all mods based PARENA based."*
      
      GFD has been **cloned and read** (`../GoblinFoxDragon`, not guessed at). What is actually in it:
      
      | Path | What it is |
      |---|---|
      | `apps/mud`, `apps2/mud` | the text MUD / state engine (jobs, combat text, progression) — **no spatial data at all** |
      | `apps2/battlegrounds_gui`, `apps/lobby` | a 3D client, the fork of SHANKPIT's lobby |
      | `packages/world/town_map.c` + `generated/town_expansion_blocks.inl` | **Town**: 17 named buildings + expansion blocks as x/z/w/d/h seeds, scale 3.0 — real geometry |
      | `data/crystal_seed_meadow.json` | **Meadow**: a 44×44 goblin *simulation* seed (goblins, kinds, grid) — **not** geometry |
      | `server/`, `server-go/`, `services/` | Go services (field office, etc.) |
      
      ## The rule that protects SHANKPIT
      
      **Nothing from GFD overwrites a SHANKPIT file.** GFD contributed data and ideas; the engine
      (XPBD `grb.c`, `structure.h`, `brick_*`, lighting, vehicles, widgets) is untouched. Where GFD had a
      parallel implementation, SHANKPIT's is the one that runs and GFD's content is imported *into* its schema.
      
      ## Phases
      
      **Phase 1 — shipped (this change).**
      - `zone_rules.prn`: the shared-zone lifecycle (900 s grace, 8 zones) and the dungeon layout numbers, all
        PARENA, with identical C defaults.
      - `zone_registry.h`: the non-instanced zone table — first entrant generates, later entrants join, expiry
        after fifteen empty minutes, re-entry inside the window keeps the layout.
      - `proc_dungeon.h`: one seed → one `CustomLevelData`, byte-identical on every machine, saved as real level
        JSON, with a gate that is a real lever → relay → machine circuit.
      - `scripts/import_gfd_levels.py`: Town → `var/maps/gfd_town.json` (boxes, perimeter, spawners). Meadow is
        reported as a sim seed, not a level, rather than fabricated.
      - Reachable: **F7** in game and `--dungeon [zone]` on the command line.**Phase 2 — shipped.** `PACKET_ZONE_STATE` (id, seed, players, state, idle_ms) plus
      `packages/simulation/zone_sync.h`: the server hosts a zone (`--dungeon [zone]`) and broadcasts once a
      second; a client decodes the packet, and reloads geometry **only** when the zone id or the seed actually
      changed, so a 1 Hz repeat never drops decals or restarts the world. The wire carries identity, not
      geometry — both sides run the same deterministic generator. `make test-zone-sync` covers the refusals
      (short datagram, wrong type, unterminated id) and the no-op-on-repeat rule.
      
      **Phase 3 — batteries-included host.** `--coop-host` that starts the authoritative server in-process (or
      as a child process) on the LAN interface, advertises over broadcast, and writes progress under `var/`.
      Single-player = the same path with nobody else joining, which is the Minecraft model the founder named.
      The current `--host/--port` client path already exists; what is missing is the host side owning both the
      UDP game loop and the zone registry.
      
      **Phase 4 — GFD state server.** Take the MUD's job/stat/inventory model, and **port its rules to PARENA**
      (`stats_bridge.prn`: job → cooldown/haste/evasion/max HP, equipment → affinities). The C side consumes a
      flat struct; it must not learn about 23 jobs. The dungeon's `difficulty` tier is the first input.
      Persistence is the state server's job (name-keyed JSON saves), not the client's.
      
      **Phase 5 — Meadow, properly.** Meadow has a *simulation* seed, not geometry. Turning it into a 3D zone
      means either authoring it as a NOCK level or teaching `proc_dungeon.h` a second layout kind (outdoor
      cells with heightfield sampling). Do that only when a scene needs it — inventing a conversion now would be
      a fake import.
      
      ## Honest state of "multiplayer"
      
      A LAN client of a `--dungeon` server now learns the zone and rebuilds the same dungeon, and reloads when
      the zone expires and regenerates. What is **not** there yet: one command that starts the host
      (`--coop-host`, phase 3), LAN discovery, and an explicit "enter zone" action — on the server, occupancy is
      whoever is connected, so the zone generates when the first client joins rather than when someone walks
      through a door. Those are the next slices, not claims.
      
- path: MONOREPO/SHANKPIT/docs/PROC_DUNGEONS.md
  content: |
      # Shared procedural zones (SHANKPIT ARCHIPELAGO, phase 1)
      
      The founder's shape, in their own words: *"like diablo where we can travel to a map and do it as a
      dungeon it can be procedurally generated ... the first person to enter it it generates and then everyone
      else enters the same one ... a grace period of 15 minutes ... dungeons are not instanced they are
      generated and then they exist until everyone leaves + 15 minutes."*
      
      This is that, built and tested, plus the GFD map import. It is **not** the whole GFD merge — see
      `docs/GFD_UNIFICATION.md` for what is still a phase.
      
      ## The three pieces
      
      | File | Owns |
      |---|---|
      | `PARENA/stdlib/shankpit/zone_rules.prn` → `packages/simulation/zone_rules.c` | every number: 900-second grace, 8 live zones, rooms/sizes/walls/doors/spawners/materials/difficulty, and the expiry predicate |
      | `packages/simulation/zone_registry.h` | the shared-zone table and its clock — enter / leave / tick, no I/O, no allocation |
      | `packages/simulation/proc_dungeon.h` | the layout: one seed → one `CustomLevelData`, saved as real level JSON |
      
      `packages/simulation/zone_rules.h` carries numerically identical C defaults so tests and any binary can
      compile without the generated file; `make test-proc-dungeon` asserts the two copies agree (over 100
      samples), the same contract `widget_rules.h` and `slide_rules.h` already keep.
      
      ## Determinism is the feature
      
      The generator uses only integer arithmetic from the rules plus an LCG seed, and every coordinate is an
      add or a multiply of small integers — no `rand()`, no float trig, no time. So:
      
      - the same seed produces **byte-identical level JSON** (the test saves two and `strcmp`s them),
      - a co-op client given the seed rebuilds the same dungeon,
      - a farmed-out dungeon that expires comes back **different**, because expiry clears the slot and the next
        entrant gets a new seed.
      
      ## Lifecycle, exactly
      
      ```
      ENTER  first entrant  -> creates the slot, gets the seed, host generates and saves the zone
             later entrants -> join the SAME slot and seed (one layout, not one per player)
             re-entry while the countdown runs -> cancels the countdown, keeps the layout
      LEAVE  drops occupancy; at zero the zone goes IDLE and starts counting. It is not deleted.
      TICK   expires a zone only when empty for >= 900 s; the host callback deletes that zone's file and the
             slot is cleared, so the next entrant generates from a new seed.
      ```
      
      An occupied zone never expires, however old it is — that is an invariant in `zone_registry_tick`, not a
      special case.
      
      ## Shape of a generated dungeon
      
      A hub plus 2–4 cardinal rooms joined by corridors, all axis-aligned, enclosed, with a ground plane. The
      hub carries a gate that is authored as a **real circuit**, not a special door type:
      
      ```
      proc_gate_lever (6 LEVER, reg 40) -> proc_gate_relay (7 DELAY, 45 ticks) -> proc_gate_motor (1 MACHINE, box_index = the gate)
      ```
      
      So the gate opens 45 ticks after the lever, through the same `widget_runtime.h` path a lab door uses, and
      the lever is the familiar `[F] USE` prompt.
      
      ## Reaching it
      
      - In game (local), **F7** descends: it creates/joins `dungeon_N` and loads it through the normal
        custom-level loader (so lighting, destructible brick, the widget circuit and zombies population all
        apply).
      - `./bin/shank_lobby --dungeon [zone]` starts straight into a generated zone.
      - `./bin/shank_server --dungeon [zone]` **hosts** one: the server owns the zone and the clock, broadcasts
        `PACKET_ZONE_STATE` (id, seed, players, state, idle_ms) at 1 Hz, and a client that receives it rebuilds
        the identical layout locally and reloads only when the id or the seed changes. No geometry crosses the
        wire — the packet carries the identity and both sides run the same deterministic generator.
      
      On the server, occupancy is the number of connected players: the first one in generates the zone, the

=== changelog head ===
## 2026-10-31

- **feat(zones): a LAN client joins the SAME procedural dungeon from its seed, not from a level transfer.** Founder: *"the first person to enter it it generates and then everyone else enters the same one"*. The server now hosts a zone: `./bin/shank_server --dungeon [zone]` generates it once, applies it through the ordinary custom-level path, and broadcasts **`PACKET_ZONE_STATE`** (`packages/common/protocol.h`, wired at 1 Hz beside the snapshot) carrying the zone id, its seed, occupancy, the registry's state and how long it has been empty. No boxes cross the wire: a client decodes the packet with the new `packages/simulation/zone_sync.h` and **rebuilds the identical layout from the seed** with the same `proc_dungeon.h` the host used, which is only sound because generation is deterministic (`make test-proc-dungeon` proves one seed writes byte-identical JSON). The reload rule is the real work: `zone_sync_should_reload` returns true only when the zone id or the seed changed, so a repeated 1 Hz packet is a no-op instead of rebuilding the world — and with it every spray, decal and cached shot — every second. Occupancy on the server is the connected player count: the first client in generates, the last one out starts the fifteen-minute countdown, expiry deletes the layout file and clears the seed, and the next arrival regenerates from a **new** seed, which is exactly what makes the clients reload. An idle zone with the same seed does not reload (it is still the same dungeon). Verified: `make test-zone-sync` (20 checks) — the packet has its own wire type, round-trips every field, and **refuses** a short datagram, the wrong type, an empty id and an unterminated id (the id becomes `var/maps/proc_<id>.json`, so that refusal is a path-safety boundary, not pedantry); the same zone at 1 Hz does not reload while a new seed does; a missing packet and an uninitialized zone never reload; an idle zone's countdown survives the wire; an absurd player count clamps instead of wrapping. Plus a **live headless server run**: `./bin/shank_server --dungeon dungeon_1` generated `PROC dungeon_1 <seed>` (41 boxes, 4 spawners, 3 materials, 3 widgets) and wrote `var/maps/proc_dungeon_1.json`, which the real parser then loaded back. That run caught a real bug this fixes: the zone id was copied into itself with `snprintf` (overlapping buffers are undefined, and glibc emptied it), so the server generated a zone and then advertised `''` and stopped broadcasting. Also `make test-proc-dungeon` (46), `test-widget-circuit` (51), `test-widget-runtime` (48), `make check-windows` (101 sources) and `make -B server`. NOT built, named: **no `--coop-host`** that starts the server in-process and advertises on the LAN (phase 3), no LAN discovery, and **no explicit "enter zone" action** — on the server, occupancy is presence, so the zone generates when the first client connects rather than when someone walks through a door.

- **feat(zones): shared, non-instanced procedural dungeons — one seed, one layout, fifteen empty minutes and then a new one.** Founder: *"we need to start unifying gfd and shankpit archipelligo ... like diablo where we can travel to a map and do it as a dungeon it can be procedurally generated ... the first person to enter it it generates and then everyone else enters the same one ... there should be a grace period of 15 minutes ... dungeons are not instanced they are generated and then they exist until everyone leaves + 15 minutes ... all mods based PARENA based"*, then *"including bringing in the GFD exclusive levels"*. GFD was **cloned and read before anything was written** (it is not in this tree, and its real contents are not what the pasted specs claimed: `apps/mud` is the text state engine with no spatial data, Town is 17 building seeds plus expansion blocks in `packages/world/town_map.c`, and Meadow is a 44×44 goblin *simulation* seed with no geometry at all — `docs/GFD_UNIFICATION.md` records this and phases the merge). Phase 1 is the deterministic zone core, in PARENA: `PARENA/stdlib/shankpit/zone_rules.prn` (generated to `packages/simulation/zone_rules.c` by `scripts/gen_zone_rules.sh` / `make regen-zone-rules`) owns the 900-second grace, 8 live zones, and every layout number — room count 3..5, sizes 24/32/40, wall height, 8-unit doors, 52-unit ring, spawners, material kind and difficulty 1..5. `packages/simulation/zone_registry.h` is the shared-zone table: **the first entrant CREATES and gets the seed, every later entrant JOINS with the same seed**, a re-entry inside the countdown cancels it and keeps the layout, an occupied zone never expires, and expiry (only at `players == 0 && idle >= 900`) clears the slot so the next entrant generates a **new** dungeon. `packages/simulation/proc_dungeon.h` builds one: a hub plus 2–4 cardinal rooms joined by corridors, axis-aligned, enclosed, ground plane, spawners, and a gate authored as a **real circuit** (lever → 45-tick relay → machine pointing at the gate's own box) rather than a bespoke door type. Determinism is the point and is tested as such: no `rand()`, no float trig, no time — two generations from one seed save **byte-identical JSON**, and a different seed does not. `scripts/import_gfd_levels.py` converts GFD's Town into `var/maps/gfd_town.json` (17 named buildings + expansion blocks at scale 3.0, a perimeter wall, materials, spawners) and says plainly that Meadow has no geometry to import. Reachable in game: **F7** descends into `dungeon_N` and `--dungeon [zone]` starts straight into one, both through the ordinary custom-level loader, so lighting, destructible brick, the widget circuit and zombies population all apply. Verified: `make test-proc-dungeon` — PARENA's rules equal the compiled-in defaults across 100+ samples (including the expiry predicate at every 50 s); the same seed builds the same box count and **identical saved bytes**; the saved level reloads through the real parser with its gate box index, circuit and spawners intact; the gate opens **on the relay's own 45-tick delay** (not on the press) through `widget_runtime`; the second entrant gets the same seed; one leave is not idle and the last leave starts the countdown; 899,999 ms is not enough and an occupied zone never expires at 9,000,000 ms; expiry calls back with the zone id, clears the slot, and the next entrant gets a different seed which produces a different dungeon; a full table refuses a ninth entry rather than sharing a stranger's world; two zones expire independently. Plus `make test-widget-circuit` (51), `make test-widget-runtime` (48), `make check-windows` (101 sources now that `widget_rules.c` and `zone_rules.c` are in `LOBBY_SRC` — a real latent link break this caught, since `main.c` had been calling `widget_rules_install()` without the generated file in the source list) and `make -B server`. NOT built, named: **no zone packet**, so a LAN friend cannot join a zone yet (the seed is host-local; phase 2), no menu tile (F7 and the CLI are the paths), no GFD state server / stat bridge (phase 4), and no Meadow level, because there is no geometry in GFD to convert.

- **feat(widgets): the circuit now RUNS in a level — F at a lever, a panel on a terminal, and a lift that actually waits.** Founder: *"general interface like F to interact and then after that it needs to be able to go into custom programmed affordances ... the main thing we are trying to do is bring the lab equipment to life ... an elevator is a widget of widgets"*, then *"focusing on delivering value and integrating it all into game modes and affordances the player actually has access to like zombies mode"*. The circuit existed and nothing called it — a lever, delay, transistor and motor were a table of numbers a test drove. New `packages/simulation/widget_runtime.h` is the host half: **plates are fed from the bodies actually standing on them** (authored radius with a vertical window, so a body six units up is not on the mat), **machines move their authored `box_index`** through the same `phys_set_custom_level_box_y` a story door uses, and **every register is mirrored into EduVM** (`eduvm_host_widget_set`), so a script's `read_sensor(reg)` and the physical switch read one number. It is deliberately free of GL, SDL, physics and the education package — the caller passes two sinks — which is what lets `make test-widget-runtime` drive the whole thing headlessly. Wired into `apps/lobby` from `lobby_edu_widgets_init`, **the same loader every custom level uses, so zombies mode, LAB and deathmatch all get it** (zombies loads through that loader, not a special path). `F` is the general interface: a lever toggles in place and **consumes the press** (so it cannot also board a vehicle on the same key), anything with a register opens its **panel**. A panel freezes movement, dials UP/DOWN in 500s, and owns ESC — leaving a panel never drops you into the pause menu. `draw_widget_affordances` draws the prompt and the panel in the existing stroke font, and the per-widget legacy box path is skipped for any box the circuit owns, so a relay's delay is real instead of two systems writing one lift. Two real bugs this run caught and fixed: the first tick of a level pushed every machine's box as a *change* (so a lift reported moving before anyone touched it — the placement now happens once, deliberately, and the test asserts it), and a terminal's dialled setpoint was **clobbered by the same tick that mirrored circuit power** (0..15) a keystroke later. A third was in my own test, not the engine: a level with no walls silently detaches `box_index` (the parser refuses a box that does not exist), which is correct behaviour the fixture had to respect. Verified: `make test-widget-runtime` (48 checks) — the first tick places both boxes once, a lever -> relay -> lift does not move for four ticks and opens on the fifth, **and does not drop early on the falling edge either**; a plate alone opens nothing while its transistor's gate lever is off, the same plate opens the door once the gate is on, stepping off closes it, a body six units above the plate never presses it, and the lift is undisturbed by plate traffic; F on a terminal opens its panel, three UP presses make 1500, five ticks later `read_sensor`'s register still holds 1500 and the mirror fired **once, on the change**; BACK returns the world, a closed panel swallows nothing, and closing it does not reset the machine; busy suppresses the prompt and walking away releases it after the hold window; a level with no widgets ticks, focuses and uses as a no-op. Plus `make test-widget-circuit` (51 checks, still green after the setpoint change), `make check-windows` and `make -B server`. NOT done, named: **no lever/centrifuge/terminal mesh** (a node is still a box coloured by its power), no editor wiring UI beyond the pin fields, a panel setpoint is display-only to a script because EduVM's widget register is boolean by contract, and there is **no widget packet** — the circuit runs in the lobby's local simulation, so a server-authoritative match would draw the boxes without the interactions.

- **feat(widgets): composable world widgets — a real circuit, an F interface, and panels that hand over to a script.** Founder: *"we already have a widget primative ... general interface like F to interact and then after that it needs to be able to go into custom programmed affordances ... the main thing we are trying to do is bring the lab equipment to life ... the widgets need to be composible ... think light switches, basic circuits, an elevator is a widget of widgets ... bring in edu vm script it all needs to play nice with that interpreter"*. The audit: the schema, the EduVM widget host and the F/BTN_USE path already existed (`LevelEduWidget`, `edu_bindings.h`, `story_buttons.h`), so this adds the missing middle — **the circuit**. `PARENA/stdlib/shankpit/widget_rules.prn` (generated to `packages/simulation/widget_rules.c` by `scripts/gen_widget_rules.sh` / `make regen-widget-rules`) defines five node kinds on one **0..15 power integer** (DEADWEIGHT's own cable tiers): LEVER (stays where you put it), PLATE (host-written sensor, a script can never forge one), DELAY (a relay — output follows input N ticks late, **both edges**), TRANSISTOR (a real AND: passes input only while its gate is powered) and MACHINE (a motor: gate, bridge, portal, crate, lift). `packages/simulation/widget_circuit.h` is the host: nodes loaded from the level, a two-phase tick in authoring order, every node's live value mirrored into its EduVM register, the proximity F prompt with hysteresis and a busy flag, and a PANEL mode that takes the keys so a script-driven affordance can own the screen. The level schema grew three keys (`input_pin`, `gate_pin`, `delay_ticks`) with `-1` defaults, and `machine_type` now accepts 6 LEVER / 7 DELAY / 8 TRANSISTOR alongside the original education machines 1..5 — a mis-wired pin is dropped at load, so a bad level degrades to "that switch does nothing", never a feedback loop. New `docs/WIDGET_AFFORDANCES.md` is the **agent-facing contract**: the JSON keys, the five kinds, and recipes for a light switch, a security door, an elevator (lever -> delay -> machine) and a lab centrifuge — which is the founder's own "a way to tell our agent to generate rich affordances". Verified: `make test-widget-circuit` — lever -> delay -> motor only runs after the relay closes **and stops late on the falling edge**; plate -> transistor -> door is a real AND (gate off closes the door with someone still standing on the plate); registers mirror live power and an unowned register reads **-1, not a fake zero**; the F prompt respects busy, picks the nearest in reach, and holds then releases; USE on a lever stays in the world while USE on a machine opens its panel; panel UP/DOWN clamp at 8000 and at 0 and BACK releases it; keys in the world are not swallowed; the PARENA curve equals the compiled-in defaults sample for sample; and bad wiring (pin past the end, empty id, unknown machine type) is dropped. Plus `make test-edu-widgets` and `make test-level-save` (the schema still round-trips). Two real problems the run caught: the first delay design only delayed the **rising** edge, which made a delay useless as a relay (both edges now, and the test asserts it), and the test target needed `gnu99` because `level_boxes.h` uses POSIX `popen`. NOT done, named: **nothing is drawn** (no prompt quad, no panel, no lever mesh), `widget_circuit_tick` is **not in the game loop yet** (the test drives it), there is **no editor wiring UI** beyond the pin fields, and DEADWEIGHT's back-EMF/overload is not modelled.

- **feat(render): metal, glass and a mirror material reflect the environment — sphere mapping, one extra draw, no assets.** Founder: *"we want to implement basic reflection in metal and glass materials i guess make a mirror material? it needs to be lightweight"*. The audit first: this renderer is fixed-function GL 1.x plus a couple of hand-loaded GL 2.0 passes (`material_shaders.h` already had specular, IPS/HPS emissive and a PARENA-tinted glass pass), so a **sphere map** is the cheap real option — the driver derives the lookup from the vertex normal and the camera basis, which means no render target, no second scene pass, no cube map, no shader and no per-frame CPU work. New `packages/render/reflection_map.h` is the environment as pixels (a pure-C, deterministic sphere map: bright sky above a warm horizon over dark ground, two cold "reflected sign" streaks, and a hot spot so a highlight visibly **travels** as you turn), and `packages/render/reflection.h` is the GL half: lazy texture creation at first use, `glTexGeni(GL_S/GL_T, GL_SPHERE_MAP)`, additive blend with depth-write off (a sheen, never an opaque coat), and a begin/end pair that **saves and restores the texture binding, texgen, blend and depth mask** — refusing a nested begin rather than corrupting its saved state. Strengths are PARENA's, not the renderer's: `mat-reflection-strength-permille(kind)` in `material_rules.prn` (**mirror 900, metal 380, glass 320, everything else 0**), so brick/concrete/wood cost exactly nothing. Wired inside `material_shaders.h` where the materials already live: `draw_material_specular_box` adds the sheen for anything at or above its own 0.6 metal threshold, `draw_material_glass_box` adds a subtle one after its transparent pass, and a new `draw_material_mirror_box` draws a near-black base so the environment IS the surface. Verified: `make test-reflection` — the map is byte-identical across builds, every texel opaque, **200+ distinct graded colours**, sky much brighter *and* bluer than the ground (so highlights are not upside-down), the hot spot 736 vs 99, the streaks visible, a degenerate size writing nothing, and the shipped strengths ordered mirror > metal > glass > 0 with an out-of-range kind reflecting nothing. Plus `make test-material-rules` (still green), `make check-windows` (99 lobby sources, which is what compiles the GL half through `material_shaders.h`) and `make -B server`. Honest limits, named: a sphere map has **no parallax** — it does not slide as you walk past and cannot reflect the actual level — so a "mirror" reads as polished chrome, not a true mirror; the real alternative costs an extra scene render per frame, which this target cannot pay. The GL state machine itself is **compiled but not run** here (no GPU, no SDL2/GL headers on this box, so the headless test covers the pixels and the numbers only), and nothing in the build yet *selects* a mirror material — `draw_material_mirror_box` exists for the material list that adds one.

- **feat(movement): a crouch-slide down a hillside now speeds you up — the same slope physics a board feels.** Founder, on the Skate spec paste: *"can we also make it so doing a slide after a slide jump in normal shankpit physics where there is a terrain like in voxworld map the slide should use the same kind of physics as the skateboarding where sliding down a hill accelerates you or whatever"*. The engine already had a slide (`apply_friction` drops to `SLIDE_FRICTION` above 0.75 units/tick while crouched) but it treated a 45 degree hillside exactly like a flat car park, because **nothing ever read the terrain normal**: a slide could only ever slow you down. Now it does, in three pieces. `PARENA/stdlib/shankpit/slide_rules.prn` (generated to `packages/simulation/slide_rules.c` by `scripts/gen_slide_rules.sh` / `make regen-slide-rules`) owns the curve as permille: how steep a face is (`(1000 - normal.y) x 3`, saturating past ~48 degrees), how much a downhill heading earns, the acceleration (constant in speed, the way gravity is), how much of the existing slide **drag** a slope keeps (`1000` on the flat — unchanged — down to 300 at full steep, because the same 1% scrub that makes a flat slide glide would otherwise cancel the hill's own pull), and the cap at 1.20 units/tick: above `MAX_SPEED`'s 0.95 on purpose, since a hill is the one way to outrun a sprint. `packages/simulation/slide_rules.h` carries numerically identical compiled-in defaults so every existing test that includes `physics.h` still links without a generated file (the test proves the two agree sample for sample), `slide_rules_host.h` installs PARENA's copy at lobby startup, and `physics.h` gains `phys_slide_slope_tick` (gravity along the surface gradient, vector-clamped to the cap) called once per tick from `local_game.h` right after `apply_friction`. Two real bugs the test caught, both mine: the heightfield normal **points against the gradient**, so my "downhill" was upside-down and a slide accelerated *uphill*; and the sub-0.75 crouch-walk scrub (90%/tick) pinned a slide that started from rest at a 0.008 crawl, so a downhill heading now uses the slide branch at any speed. Verified: `make test-slide-slope` — a real 1:1 (45 degree) heightfield sampled through the engine's own `terrain_sample_normal`: **one tick of a flat slide is exactly the old formula to 1e-5, the slope step never fires on flat ground, and a flat slide still comes to rest**; a downhill slide reaches 1.09 after 60 ticks against 0.00 on the flat (and outruns `MAX_SPEED`), pinned at exactly 1.20 after 120 ticks, accelerating along the downhill axis; a slide from rest on a hill starts moving; an uphill slide never gains speed, stalls, and is turned back downhill; airborne/standing/in-vehicle all no-op; and PARENA's curve equals the header's defaults across 3,608 samples. Plus `make test-wall-ride` (the existing airborne wall ride is untouched), `make check-windows` (98 lobby sources) and `make -B server`. NOT done, named: **terrain only** — a rotated box ramp has a face normal per box rather than a field under the player, so a slide on an authored ramp gets nothing yet; the server installs no PARENA copy (its compiled-in defaults are the same numbers, and the test enforces that equality, but a future retune would reach the lobby first); and the rest of the pasted Skate spec (dual-stick flick detection, third-person orbit, grind snapping, manuals) is **not** in this change — this is the slide-on-a-hill half the founder actually asked for.

- **feat(anim): the thirteen-clip animation set gets a decision and a naming contract — the ragdoll half of the spec already existed.** Founder paste: the Mixamo + XPBD ragdoll engineering spec. The audit changed what got built: **§4 (ragdoll) is already done and wired** — `packages/simulation/ragdoll_pool.h` runs 17 Winter/Dempster-mass segments on GOLDENBAND's grb XPBD solver with per-death-kind timings from PARENA, and `apps/lobby/src/main.c` already spawns, steps, evicts and skins them on death (`g_rd_pool`, `ragdoll_pool_get_skin_matrices`). **§2/§3 did not exist at all**: nothing decided *which* clip a tick belongs to (the player's body is drawn procedurally by `compute_player_anim_pose`, and NPC kits only know AUTO/GREET/DANCE), and no clip-naming contract existed for an imported rig to satisfy — so an importer had nothing to conform to and no way to fail loudly. New `PARENA/stdlib/shankpit/anim_rules.prn` (generated to `packages/simulation/anim_rules.c` by `scripts/gen_anim_rules.sh` / `make regen-anim-rules`) is the decision, in a priority order the spec leaves out and a player notices immediately: **melee swing > ability > fire > reload > airborne (jump-start for its own 6-tick window, then in-air, plus the reserved climb state) > crouch/slide > walk/run/idle by speed band**. It also owns the metadata a state machine needs and a spec dump usually forgets: which states loop (exactly the six postures — a looping reload is the classic bug), that **only the recoil is upper-body additive** so a player can shoot while running, a per-state crossfade (60 ms for a shot, 150 for a posture), the walk/run bands, the melee windows (**20 knife / 28 katana / 42 hammer**, matching `protocol.h`'s own weapon table so the clip window and the damage window are one number), and the eye height. New `packages/simulation/anim_state.h` is the host: it reads only real `PlayerState` fields (`on_ground`, `crouching`, `vx/vz`, `jump_timer`, `is_shooting`, `reload_timer`, `katana_slash_timer`, `dash_timer`), maps `WPN_*` to the three melee classes, and publishes the **clip-name contract** (`anim_idle` … `anim_climb_loop`, thirteen unique lowercase stems that become `<asset>/<name>.gband`) so an importer renames its Mixamo clips or fails at load instead of silently playing the idle for everything. Two honest corrections to the spec, named rather than copied: its crouch eye heights (4.0 → 2.5) are from a different build — this engine's is `EYE_HEIGHT` 2.59, and the test **asserts the rule equals that constant** (via a one-function probe TU, `anim_engine_constant.c`, because `physics.h` carries unused statics that would trip this repo's `-Werror`) — and its `ANIM_SLIDE` has **no real producer here**: this engine's crouch-slide is a friction change and the wall ride is ctrl-in-air, neither sets a timer, so `slide_ticks` is an explicit caller argument rather than an invented field. Verified: `make test-anim-state` — 90 checks: every state has a name and no two share one, an out-of-range state falls back to idle instead of null, band edges land exactly at their thresholds (59 idle / 60 walk / 299 walk / 300 run), backwards movement is RUN not IDLE, crouch owns locomotion at any speed, jump-start ends exactly at its window and a walk-off falls straight to IN_AIR, **a swing outranks firing and reloading, and firing survives being airborne**, an ability outranks a slide, exactly six postures loop and all seven actions are one-shots, a shot blends faster than a posture, knife/katana/hammer windows match the real weapon ids while a rifle has none, the standing eye height equals the engine's own, and the real `PlayerState` wrapper drives IDLE/RUN/CROUCH/FIRE/RELOAD/MELEE/JUMP from those fields (a diagonal is 0.424 units/tick, not 0.6). Also `make check-windows` (98 lobby sources compile for mingw) and `make -B server`. NOT done, stated plainly: **nothing is drawn from this yet** — no imported skin has these thirteen clips on disk, the kit loader still takes four clip names (idle/walk/greet/dance) rather than thirteen, and the player draw path is still procedural; `anim_state.h` is not included by `main.c` yet, so the mingw check proves `anim_rules.c` compiles, not that the header does on Windows. There is also no `.gband`-from-Mixamo importer in this repo (the spec's Blender script does not exist here), so the mapping is a contract to import *into*, not a converter.

- **feat(bedrockracers): the stadium exists natively, and its mesh is checked against the surface the car is clamped to.** Founder: *"implement bedrock racers in the native shankpit client pixel for pixel using shankpit unified physics ... also the geometry of the level needs to be accurate with the smooth curved walls"* and *"we need to dedupe stuff into parena as much as possible so the bedrock racers wasm stuff leaks into shankpit"*. The shape is **PARENA's**, not a re-derived C copy: `PARENA/stdlib/bedrockracers/web/br_stadium.prn` (generated to `packages/simulation/br_stadium.c` by `scripts/gen_br_stadium.sh` / `make regen-br-stadium`) holds the exact rounded box the web game drives on — 520 × 520 in plan, 240 tall, **a 70-unit fillet on every edge**, the four upside-down goal shafts at ±450, and the rally loop's own scale/width so the road baked into BR's floor texture and the road this client draws come from one pair of constants. New `packages/simulation/br_stadium.h` is the native half: the SDF query (positive = air inside the room), the surface normal as the SDF's gradient by central difference (**continuous**, which is the entire reason wall-riding works: floor → fillet → wall → ceiling has no seam, where a faceted shell would give 12 normals per turn), the fan-grip curve, and an **exact** mesh — six flat faces inset by the radius, twelve quarter-cylinder edges, eight eighth-sphere corners. `packages/render/br_stadium_gl.h` draws it through the same immediate-mode GL path every world box already uses (no textures, no GLSL, no VBO), with a per-vertex tint so the curl reads. Wired into `LOBBY_SRC` and `SERVER_SRC` so the client that draws it and the server that collides with it link the same numbers. Verified: `make test-br-stadium` — the floor/ceiling/walls are on the surface and 5 units inside or outside are open air or solid respectively, a 45-degree point on the fillet returns a clean 45-degree normal, normals are unit length, **all 416 vertices of the quality-4 shell sit within 0.0000 of the SDF and every stored normal matches the gradient to a dot of 1.0000** (the property that stops a car driving through a wall it appears to touch), quality 6 is 936 quads, an absurd quality fills the pool instead of overrunning it, grip is weak when crawling and total from 2.0 units/tick, and the draw path receives exactly four vertices per quad in one batch. Two real bugs the test caught and this fixes: the grip curve *exceeded* 1000 permille between 400 and 1400 units/tick, and flipping the edge normals to point into the air also flipped the component the edge **position** used, pulling every fillet vertex 70 units into the wall. Also learned and named: this repo's PARENA emitter lowers only `I32`/`F64`/`Bool`/`String`, so the shape module is `F64` (`F32` refused to compile), written as small `defn`s rather than one `let` because the emitter's `let` binds typed scalars only. NOT done, and named rather than implied: **the stadium is not in any scene yet** — nothing builds the mesh at load, nothing draws it, no car is clamped to it, and there is no collision response, no goal-tower shafts in the SDF, and no faceted OBB destruction shell; the four goal towers are exported as numbers and nothing more. `docs/` carries no northstar for this yet, and no visual claim is possible here (no GPU or display).

- **feat(render): the Doom/Quake/Half-Life/GTA material vocabulary, as rules instead of a shader rewrite.** Founder paste (a spec dump proposing a `#version 330` PBR/VBO/voxel-lightmap pipeline) then: *"what other materials/shaders do we need for full doom/quake/half life/gta story telling?"* and *"anything missing from source 2 engine?"*. The audit came first and it changed the answer: SHANKPIT is fixed-function GL 1.x plus **one hand-loaded GL 2.0 shader path** (`gl_shader.h`, the flashlight beam and the fireball), so `#version 330 core`, VAOs, `sampler3D`/`glTexImage3D`, `glVertexAttribIPointer` and a deferred G-buffer **cannot compile or run here** — all named in `docs/RENDER_NORTHSTAR.md` §4, along with the pasted shader's fake PBR term and its claim of bit-identical GPU timing. What a story actually needs from a material is *animation*, so that is what was built, in PARENA where it can be deterministic: `PARENA/stdlib/shankpit/material_rules.prn` (generated into `packages/simulation/material_rules.c`, `make regen-material-rules`) — five material kinds (plain, scrolling, frame-loop, palette-LUT, emissive-flicker) with **UV scroll speeds that wrap on the second** and a vertical component so ooze reads as thick, **frame-loop sheets** (`mat-frame-index(fps, frames, tick)`) for terminals/cameras/bomb timers, **all eight Quake light styles** (steady, strobe, unstable fluorescent, broken tube, pulse, dying, alarm, candle) as 0..1000 permille of a fixture's brightness, emissive faces floored so a lit terminal still reads in a bright room, the four screen tints (low health, submerged, acid, shield), a 256-entry palette wrap that never goes negative, and `vlm-axis-index-milli` — the clamped integer mapping that is the honest half of Source 2's `M_combined_light_probe_volume` (a baked grid sampled per face, not a 3D texture this build cannot bind). Verified: `make test-material-rules` (every style stays in 0..1000 over 600 ticks; the strobe really goes dark and really lights; the fluorescent drops out 1-19 times in 10 s; the broken tube is dark more than twice as often as lit; snaps and frames wrap on the second; all 8 frames of a 10 fps sheet are reached; health tint is 0 at full and monotonic in damage; submerged saturates; palette -1 wraps to 255 and 300 to 44; probe axes clamp at both ends and mid-grid), plus `make check-windows` (96 lobby sources) and `make -B server`. NOT done, and named in the doc: **nothing of this is drawn yet** — no probe bake, no UV-offset draw path, no palette LUT shader, no tint quad wiring, and no visual verification is possible here (no GPU/display). The doc ranks the build order and says plainly that a real palette shader is the only genuinely new fragment program the list needs.
- **feat(empire): influence is a currency you spend on bodies, and the map is a sphere of districts.** Founder: *"clone down EMPIRE ... clone down ECOWAR ... clone down REDGARDEN ... clone down TRAPX ... we need phone app affordances in shankpit to bring in the mp and to clone your troops in PARENA first mods based it should show the minimap of the nearby area and allow you to spawn in troops near you or near buildings you have enough influence over ... in empire mode the map itself should be a big sphere and it should be procedurally generated"*. All four repos cloned and read before writing anything (`docs/EMPIRE_NORTHSTAR.md` records what each one actually contains, which is not what their names suggest: EMPIRE is a bridge + deck UI with no world, ECOWAR is the arena game with 16 tested cards and **no in-match deck UI**, REDGARDEN holds the team AI and hero kits, TRAPX is the doctrine — alignment and pressure on a grid, no avatar, no direct unit control). Rules first, as asked: `PARENA/stdlib/shankpit/empire_rules.prn` (generated into `packages/simulation/empire_rules.c` by `scripts/gen_empire_rules.sh` / `make regen-empire-rules`) defines **one currency** — influence at 2/s capped at 400, four troop kinds (25/35/40/60), a **clone at 130% of a recruit** that needs a veteran to copy, a squad cap of 6, a 14-unit spawn radius, TRAPX's three-way district alignment (yours/neutral/rival at 600‰ pressure) with income attached (full, a third, none), and **the sphere: 6/12/18/18/12/6 = 72 districts**, ring counts rising to the equator so districts keep their area — the reason a sphere beats a lat/long grid, where the phone's minimap would lie at the poles. New phone app **`BP_APP_EMPIRE`** (P → EMPIRE): a nine-cell minimap of the nearby districts (yours blue, rival red, yours-to-stand-on green) and the spawn/clone rows, painted as HTML+CSS by the same PELLEGRINO surface the kit pages use, with a real text fallback so the app is never a blank rectangle. The phone **never spends**: SELECT emits `BP_FX_EMPIRE_SPAWN`/`_CLONE` and the host re-checks the same PARENA gate (`empire_can_spawn`/`empire_clone_can`) before taking the influence and placing a body 2 units beside the player, so a retuned cost cannot let the UI and the world disagree. Verified: `make test-empire-rules` (costs, the clone premium, refusal at one point short, unknown kinds, the squad cap, clone-needs-a-veteran, district flip/income, 72 districts with the equator ring larger than the pole cap, spawn radius local), `make test-vehicle-burn`, `phone_test` (the app list still covers every app), `make check-windows` (96 lobby sources) and `make -B server`. Named, not faked: **the body is a story-AI slot, not a loyal soldier** — SHANKPIT has bodies and REDGARDEN has the friendly/enemy team model, and nothing yet joins them, so the placement is real and the allegiance is not; **no district simulation exists in the world**, so the minimap honestly shows you holding the block you stand on and its neighbours neutral; **the sphere is geometry only** — no procedural city generation and no streaming yet; and there is no wire format, so influence and ownership are single-player state.
- **feat(nock): every vehicle is placeable in a map — IDUNA NOCK, local NOCK, and the native loader.** Founder: *"we need nock affordances for spawning all the new vehicles in a map including iduna nock including local nock we already have a widget for buggy spawnerer"*. The buggy tile was the right idea with one vehicle in it. Its name convention is now the general case: **`vehicle_spawn_<kind>` / `vehicle_spawn_<kind>_<deg>`** with kind `buggy`, `rocket`, `heli`, `recon`, `fly`, `plane` — one thin wall, no schema change, so select/undo/clone/glTF/widget-flattening all keep working, and a **legacy `buggy_spawn` tile still works and is ALSO exported as kind `buggy`**, so nothing authored before this moves. IDUNA (`level_store.go`): `VehicleSpawnExport` + `vehicleSpawnsForExport` (max 24) alongside the untouched buggy list, `rotatedVehicleSpawnName` carries a placed widget's rotation into the spawn's yaw (a legacy buggy tile stays a legacy buggy tile), and the two flatten call sites now go through it. Native (`packages/world/level_boxes.h`): `LevelVehicleSpawn` + `vehicle_spawns` parsed and re-written (so `--edit-map` F6 round-trips it), with `LEVEL_VEHICLE_*` kinds and human aliases. `physics.h` gains one `g_custom_level_vehicle_*` set beside the buggy arrays; both `apps/server` and `apps/lobby` copy it through; and `local_game.h`'s one `scene_load(SCENE_CUSTOM_LEVEL)` places the whole roster where the map says — buggy/rocket into a `BuggyState` (`.rocket = 1` for the rocket car), heli into a hovers-ready `HelicopterState`, recon/fly into `DroneState` at their own kind, plane on the apron. Both editors got the affordance: IDUNA's level editor and widget editor each gain a kind `<select>` + **Add vehicle spawn** (a coloured pad per kind, so a garage bay reads at a glance), and local NOCK's canvas editor gains a **Vehicle** tool (key `v`), draws every placed spawn in its kind's colour, saves them into the level JSON, and mirrors the game's own placements from the new `vehicle_spawn` event (added to local NOCK's event allow-list). Verified: `make test-level-save` (the new list round-trips through the native writer/loader) and `make check-windows` compiling every lobby source. NOT verified: the IDUNA Go/TypeScript builds — this sandbox has no `go` or SDL2 — so those edits are reviewed, not compiled; and no live match was driven, so a placed C-110 is placed on the apron but has not been seen flying from a map yet.
- **feat(vehicles): a car smokes, catches fire, and only then blows up — drawn with Bedrock Racers' fire.** Founder: *"use the shaders from bedrock racers on fire for when a car is about to blow up or whatever"*. The look is not invented: `PARENA/stdlib/shankpit/vehicle_burn_rules.prn` (generated to `packages/simulation/vehicle_burn_rules.c` by `scripts/gen_vehicle_burn_rules.sh` / `make regen-vehicle-burn-rules`, installed at startup by `vehicle_burn_rules_host.h`) copies BR's `br_fx.prn` fire curve — **fire-fx swells 25% of the remaining gap per tick (fx-fire-rise) and dies at 6% (fx-fire-fall)**, its light flickers between 1.4 and 2.4 "a car's worth", and its drama scalar jumps then ebbs — and adds the ladder BR does not have: hull ≤ 150 smokes, hull ≤ 75 is on fire, and the 75 points between the fire line and zero take **exactly 300 ticks (5 s)** at 0.25 hp/tick, so the warning window and the burn clock are the same number instead of two guesses. `packages/simulation/vehicle_burn.h` is the per-tick state machine (`vehicle_burn_tick` returns the ONE tick the car detonates; `vehicle_burn_light`/`vehicle_burn_drama` carry BR's flicker deterministically from the car's seed and tick; crash damage is mass × delta-v², staged to stay inside i32, ~22 of 300 hull for a full-speed buggy — reckless a few times, not fatal once). The lobby draws a burning buggy with the **same additive fireball shader the grenade/missile blast already uses** (`fireball_draw`, two billboards, sized by `fire_fx`), and the blast itself is the existing `fx_spawn_explosion` path. Two real bugs the new test caught and this fixes: the burn clock was inconsistent with the fire line when it was whole points per tick, and **the fire latched on `burning_ticks`, so a repaired car burned forever** — it is now a function of the hull, and a repair puts it out and restarts the fuse. Limitation, named: the hull and the blast are the local/client sim's — there is no wire field for a burning car yet, so a networked match does not replicate the fire state, and smoke is modelled (and tested) but drawn only as the flame's arrival, not as its own dark plume.

New `packages/simulation/airplane_flight.h` is the integration: throttle is a **lever** (SPACE up, CTRL down, it holds where you leave it), W/S elevator, A/D aileron, the pilot's heading is a tiller only with the wheels down and slow, and **a bank is what turns it** — every rate is heavy, so it turns like a transport and not like a quad. Two new rules in `drone_rules.prn` (regenerated): `drone-shard-kills(kind, mass-grams, rel-speed-milli)` — **any** shard with mass kills the 45 g micro, while the recon's frame needs `mass x relative speed > 40,000,000` (a 15 kg chunk doing ~2.7 units/tick, about what the top of a collapse moves), so dust and pebbles bounce off it — and `drone-gimbal-yaw/pitch-milli` — the recon's head swings **90°** with **60°** of pitch, the micro's 20°/25°. New host side in `drone_flight.h`: `drone_shard_contact()` (point shard vs the airframe's own radius, 1.2 m recon / 0.35 m micro, deciding through the rule), `drone_kill()`, `drone_eject_pilot()` (thrown clear where it died, falling, not riding a wreck), and `drone_gimbal_track()`/`drone_gimbal_view_yaw()` (the offset clamped to the airframe's mechanical limits, because a gimbal is a mechanism and not free look). `DroneState` gains `destroyed`, `gimbal_yaw`, `gimbal_pitch`. Wired in the lobby: `drone_shard_sweep()` runs every frame over the live debris (`g_brick_debris`, the flakes a cracking wall throws — this build has no simulated structural shards, so mass is estimated from each flake's own volume and its per-SECOND velocity converted to the per-TICK flight model), a hit ejects the pilot and fires a real fireball (0.6 units for the micro, 1.6 for the recon); and the mouse now drives the drone's head through `drone_gimbal_clamp()` instead of a free camera. ## What `--coop-host` does now

`./bin/shank_lobby --coop-host [zone]` is one command that hosts and plays:

1. `packages/simulation/coop_host.c` finds `bin/shank_server` the same way every other launcher does (`bundled/` first, then the dev tree) and starts it with `--port 6969 --dungeon <zone>` — fork/exec on POSIX, `CreateProcessA(CREATE_NO_WINDOW)` on Windows, matching `lobby_launch_nock`.
2. The client points at loopback and enters **`MODE_QUEUE`** via the same `reset_client_render_state_for_net(); net_connect();` path the menu's TDM tile uses. The host is a networked player, not a local special case, so an ally joins with `--host <host-lan-ip>` and both sides run identical netcode. It is deliberately **not** the existing `--dungeon`, which builds the zone in-process and has no server anyone can reach — that flag could never be co-op.

Two decisions carry the weight:

- **The UDP port probe.** UDP has no `accept`, so the helper binds the port briefly and lets go. That is what makes relaunching *attach* to a world that is still up rather than spawning a second server that cannot bind and dies — and it is why quitting and re-entering the same dungeon works.
- **Zone ids are validated at the flag** (`[A-Za-z0-9_-]`, never leading `-`). The id is a real filename component (`var/maps/proc_<zone>.json`) *and* an argv element; one unchecked string, two injection surfaces. A failure never overwrites `SERVER_HOST`/`SERVER_PORT`, so a bad binary or refused bind leaves you in the lobby with the reason on screen instead of silently connecting to the internet default.

## Checks actually run

- **`make test-coop-host` — 40 checks, 0 failed.** Defaults are the server's own defaults; a zone with a slash, `..`, a leading `-`, a space, a dot or backslash is refused, as are privileged and out-of-range ports; the child argv is exactly `{ bin, --port, 6969, --dungeon, <zone>, NULL }`. The probe reads free, **busy against a socket the test really binds**, then free again. Then the live part: the test calls the same `coop_host_start` the lobby calls, gets a pid, **waits for `var/maps/proc_coop_selftest.json` to appear** (the server's own output, not the fork's exit code), confirms the port is held, confirms a **second start attaches instead of spawning a twin**, stops it, and confirms the port is released.
- **Windows cross-compile**: the entire `apps/lobby/src/main.c` compiles under `x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc` with these edits — exit 0, no errors; `coop_host.c` alone clean under `-Wextra -Werror`.

## Limits, stated plainly

- **The client wiring was compiled, not run.** `make lobby` cannot link on this box at all — `../EDITOR.GAME` isn't checked out and there are no native SDL2 headers — and there's no display, so no live `--coop-host` session was driven. The spawn/it's-a-real-server half *is* exercised by the test; the "and then the window connects" half is not.
- **No LAN discovery.** An ally types the host's IP; nothing announces the world.
- **The server outlives the lobby.** It's a child process, so quitting the host leaves the world up until it's killed. Deliberate for now (a hosted world surviving one person's session is the point), but it's a policy that needs your call.
- No in-process host.

`docs/GFD_UNIFICATION.md` now marks phase 3 shipped with those gaps named, `docs/PROC_DUNGEONS.md` lists the command beside `--dungeon`, and the CHANGELOG entry records the test numbers.

  "content": "/* zone_beacon.h -- LAN discovery for a hosted world: \"there is a dungeon at 192.168.1.20:6969\".\n *\n * The last named gap in docs/GFD_UNIFICATION.md phase 3. `--coop-host` made hosting one command, but\n * the ally still had to be told an IP, which is exactly the friction the founder's \"potentially a lan\n * ally could join for coop on our world\" is about. Nothing here authenticates anything -- a beacon is\n * an advertisement, and the truthful source address of the datagram is the address worth dialling, so\n * a forged one can only point a player at a host that will not answer. That is deliberate: a\n * discovery protocol with trust in it is a much bigger thing than \"find the world on this LAN\".\n *\n * This is NOT part of the game protocol (packages/common/protocol.h): it travels on its own UDP port,\n * to nobody in particular, is never required for a session to work, and carries identity only -- the\n * same discipline as PACKET_ZONE_STATE, which sends a zone's (id, seed) and lets both sides generate\n * the geometry. A beacon that says the wrong port would send allies to nothing, so the game port is\n * carried explicitly rather than assumed to be 6969.\n */\n#ifndef SHANKPIT_ZONE_BEACON_H\n#define SHANKPIT_ZONE_BEACON_H\n\n#define ZONE_BEACON_MAGIC 0x53505A42u /* \"SPZB\", little-endian on the wire */\n#define ZONE_BEACON_VERSION 1\n#define ZONE_BEACON_PORT 6968 /* one below the game port; nothing else in this tree uses it */\n#define ZONE_BEACON_SIZE 48   /* fixed: a beacon is small, and a variable one invites length bugs */\n#define ZONE_BEACON_ZONE_MAX 32\n#define ZONE_BEACON_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS 3000\n\ntypedef struct {\n    char zone[ZONE_BEACON_ZONE_MAX];\n    unsigned int seed;\n    int players;\n    int port; /* the UDP game port this world actually listens on */\n} ZoneBeacon;\n\n/* Serialise to exactly ZONE_BEACON_SIZE bytes. Returns the length, or 0 if the beacon is not\n * advertisable (bad zone id, port out of range) or `out` is too small. */\nint zone_beacon_encode(const ZoneBeacon *b, unsigned char *out, int out_sz);\n\n/* Treat the datagram as untrusted input: wrong length, magic or version, an empty/unterminated/\n * illegal zone id, or an out-of-range port are all refused rather than half-decoded. */\nint zone_beacon_decode(const unsigned char *in, int len, ZoneBeacon *out);\n\n/* Send one beacon to the LAN broadcast address AND to loopback. The broadcast is the LAN's copy; the\n * loopback copy is for the host's own finder, and it is what lets a discovery test run on a box with\n * no broadcast route (this one). Returns the number of sends that succeeded (0..2). */\nint zone_beacon_announce(int sock, int beacon_port, const ZoneBeacon *b);\n\n/* An announce socket: UDP, SO_BROADCAST, SO_REUSEADDR (a restarted host must be able to re-advertise\n * immediately). Returns -1 on failure. Close it with zone_beacon_close. */\nint zone_beacon_socket(void);\nvoid zone_beacon_close(int sock);\n\n/* Wait up to `timeout_ms` for a beacon. On success fills `out`, and `source_ip` with the datagram's\n * real source address (the address to dial) -- never a field from inside the packet. Returns 1 on a\n * world found, 0 on timeout, -1 if the beacon port could not be bound. */\nint zone_beacon_find(int beacon_port, int timeout_ms, ZoneBeacon *out, char *source_ip, int ip_sz);\n\n#endif /* SHANKPIT_ZONE_BEACON_H */\n"
}

      static void server_zone_begin(const char *zone) {
          const char *id = (zone && zone[0]) ? zone : "dungeon_1";
          unsigned int seed = 0;
          int created;
          if (!g_server_zones_ready) {
              zone_registry_init(&g_server_zones, (unsigned int)get_server_time() | 1u);
              g_server_zones_ready = 1;
          }
          created = zone_registry_enter(&g_server_zones, id, (int)get_server_time(), &seed);
          if (created < 0) { printf("[ZONE] no free slot for '%s'\n", id); g_server_zone_id[0] = 0; return; }
          g_server_zone_seen_players = 1;   /* the first tick with nobody connected releases it to idle */
          server_zone_generate_and_apply(id, seed);
      }
      
      void server_broadcast_zone_state(void) {
          static unsigned int last_ms = 0;
          unsigned int now_ms = get_server_time();
          int connected = 0, state;
          NetZoneState pkt;
      
          if (!g_server_zones_ready || !g_server_zone_id[0]) return;
          for (int i = 1; i < MAX_CLIENTS; i++)

          state = zone_registry_state(&g_server_zones, g_server_zone_id);

              unsigned int seed = 0;
              if (zone_registry_enter(&g_server_zones, g_server_zone_id, (int)now_ms, &seed) == 1)
                  server_zone_generate_and_apply(g_server_zone_id, seed);
          } else if (connected > g_server_zone_seen_players) {
              for (int n = g_server_zone_seen_players; n < connected; n++)
                  zone_registry_enter(&g_server_zones, g_server_zone_id, (int)now_ms, NULL);
          } else if (connected < g_server_zone_seen_players) {
              for (int n = connected; n < g_server_zone_seen_players; n++)
                  zone_registry_leave(&g_server_zones, g_server_zone_id, (int)now_ms);

      "newString": "## 2026-10-31\n\n- **feat(zones): a world announces itself on the LAN, so an ally runs `--coop-find` instead of being told an IP.** The last named gap in phase 3: `--coop-host` made hosting one command, but the joiner still needed an address typed at them. New `packages/simulation/zone_beacon.{h,c}`: a **fixed 48-byte** beacon (magic, version, game port, players, seed, NUL-padded zone id), announced by the server on the **same 1 Hz beat as `PACKET_ZONE_STATE`** to the broadcast address **and to loopback** — the broadcast is the LAN's copy, and the loopback copy is what lets the host's own finder see its world and what makes the discovery test run on a box with no broadcast route. It carries **identity only**, exactly like the zone packet: a joiner still generates the dungeon locally from the seed, so nothing about the geometry is transferred and the beacon stays 48 bytes forever. `zone_beacon_find` binds the beacon port, waits with a 100 ms `select` loop, and drops anything that is not a valid beacon (that port is open to every process on the LAN) — and the address it returns is the **datagram's source**, never a field inside the packet, so a forged beacon can only point a player at a host that will not answer. The id rule is shared with `--coop-host` (`coop_host_zone_valid`) rather than restated, because the decodable id is still a filename on the receiving side (`var/maps/proc_<id>.json`). Server: `--beacon-port N` (0 disables advertising), announced only while the zone is live, and it advertises `g_server_game_port` — the port this process actually bound, not the constant 6969, since a beacon pointing at 6969 while the world runs elsewhere sends allies to nothing. Client: `--coop-find [beacon-port]` listens, then joins the same `MODE_QUEUE` path the host uses. Verified: `make test-zone-beacon` — **33 checks, 0 failed**: encode/decode round-trips zone, seed, players and port; reserved bytes stay zero; and the refusals are the real work — a short, over-long, NULL or wrong-magic datagram, a future version, an empty id, an **unterminated** id (no NUL inside its field), an id that is a path (`../etc`), an id that looks like a flag (`-rf`), game port 0 and a privileged port are all refused; a too-small encode buffer and an invalid zone/port are never advertised; a negative player count clamps to 0 instead of wrapping into the packet. Then the live half: the test starts the actual server on `--port 7351 --beacon-port 7352`, waits for it to write its zone, calls the same `zone_beacon_find` the client calls, and asserts it heard the world **named the one that is running**, with **the real game port**, a sane player count, the seed, and a source address that parses as IPv4. `make test-coop-host` still 40/40 (the server source list gained `zone_beacon.c`/`coop_host.c`), and the whole client `main.c` (with `--coop-find` wired) cross-compiles for mingw with no errors. NOT verified, named: **the client's own find-and-connect was compiled, not run** — `make lobby` cannot link here (`../EDITOR.GAME` absent, no native SDL2 headers) and there is no display, so the live proof is the server-side beacon plus the finder, not a joiner's window. Discovery is also **same-broadcast-domain only** (no relay, no internet lobby), and the beacon says nothing about map identity beyond the zone id and seed — a host running a hand-authored `--level` advertises only its zone.\n\n- **feat(zones): hosting a LAN world is one command",

    }

}

Pushed as **`6f99ee0`**; `master` is level with origin.

## What shipped

An ally no longer needs an address read to them.

**Server side** — `packages/simulation/zone_beacon.{h,c}` sends a fixed **48-byte** identity beacon at the same 1 Hz beat as `PACKET_ZONE_STATE`, to the broadcast address *and* to loopback. The loopback copy is not decoration: it's how the host's own finder sees its world, and it's what makes this testable on a box with no broadcast route. It carries `zone id`, `seed`, `players`, and **the game port this process actually bound** — deliberately not the constant 6969, because a beacon advertising 6969 while the world runs on 7351 sends allies to nothing. Announced only while the zone is live; `--beacon-port 0` hosts privately.

**Client side** — `--coop-find [beacon-port]` listens, then joins through the same `MODE_QUEUE` path the host uses.

**Discovery is identity only, exactly like the zone packet.** No geometry crosses the wire; a joiner still generates the dungeon locally from the seed, which is why the beacon can stay 48 bytes forever. Two choices carry the security weight: the address to dial is the **datagram's source**, never a field inside the packet (a forged beacon can only point you at a host that won't answer), and the zone-id rule is *shared* with `--coop-host` rather than restated, because the decoded id is still a filename on the receiving side. A beacon port that fails or is disabled cannot affect a session that already works.

## Checks actually run

- **`make test-zone-beacon` — 33 checks, 0 failed.** Round-trips zone/seed/players/port, reserved bytes stay zero; then the refusals, which are the real work: short, over-long, NULL, wrong-magic, future-version, empty id, **unterminated** id, an id that is a path (`../etc`), an id that looks like a flag (`-rf`), game port 0, privileged port; a too-small encode buffer and an invalid zone/port are never advertised; a negative player count clamps instead of wrapping. Then the live half: a real `bin/shank_server` on `--port 7351 --beacon-port 7352`, the finder the client calls hears it, names the running world, reports the **real** game port, the seed, and an IPv4 source address.
- **`make test-coop-host` — still 40/40** after the server source list gained `zone_beacon.c`/`coop_host.c` (regression, not assumed).
- **Windows**: whole client `main.c` with `--coop-find` wired compiles under mingw (exit 0, zero errors); `zone_beacon.c` clean under `-Wextra -Werror`.

## Limits

- **The joiner's own client was compiled, not run.** `make lobby` can't link on this box at all — `../EDITOR.GAME` isn't checked out and there are no native SDL2 headers — and there's no display. The live proof is the server's beacon plus the finder, not a second window connecting.
- **Same broadcast domain only.** No relay, no internet lobby.
- **The server still outlives the lobby** (child process). That policy is still your call, and it's the next thing I'd want decided rather than guessed.

`docs/GFD_UNIFICATION.md` marks discovery shipped with those gaps named, `docs/PROC_DUNGEONS.md` documents both commands, and the CHANGELOG carries the test numbers.

- path: MONOREPO/PARENA/stdlib/shankpit/zone_rules.prn
  content: |
      ;; stdlib/shankpit/zone_rules.prn -- shared (instanceless) world zones and their procedural layouts.
      ;;
      ;; Founder: "we need to start unifying GFD and shankpit ... i want to make it so that GFD server we have
      ;; it like diablo where we can travel to a map and do it as a dungeon it can be procedurally generated
      ;; ... for now the first person to enter it it generates and then everyone else enters the same one ...
      ;; there should be a grace period of 15 minutes for the zone existing for after you leave it ... dungeons
      ;; are not instanced they are generated and then they exist until everyone leaves + 15 minutes".
      ;;
      ;; So there are two separate things here and they are deliberately not the same file:
      ;;   * the LIFECYCLE (how long an empty zone survives) is pure arithmetic on two integers -- this module,
      ;;     so the client, the server and the test cannot disagree about the grace period;
      ;;   * the LAYOUT (how many rooms, how big, which material) is generation parameters, also here, so a
      ;;     seed produces the same dungeon on every machine that runs this build.
      ;;
      ;; Every function is I32 and total: no state, no allocation, no RNG hidden inside. The caller owns the
      ;; seed and the clock (packages/simulation/zone_registry.h), which is what makes a zone reproducible and
      ;; a test possible. All millisecond values are milliseconds.
      (module shankpit/zone-rules)
      (export zone-grace-seconds zone-max-zones
              zone-room-count zone-room-width zone-room-depth zone-wall-height
              zone-wall-thickness zone-door-width zone-ring-distance
              zone-ring-dir-x zone-ring-dir-z
              zone-spawn-count zone-mob-count zone-material-count zone-material-for
              zone-difficulty zone-zone-status-name
              zone-should-expire zone-elapsed-ms)
      
      ;; zr-clamp, NOT w-clamp: PARENA lowers a helper to a global C function, and widget_rules.prn already
      ;; defines w_clamp -- two modules with the same helper name is a duplicate-symbol link error, found live.
      (defn zr-clamp [(lo : I32) (hi : I32) (x : I32)] : I32 (if (< x lo) lo (if (> x hi) hi x)))
      
      ;; The founder's own number: fifteen minutes of nobody inside and the layout is gone, so a farmed-out
      ;; zone does not come back the way it was.
      (defn zone-grace-seconds [] : I32 900)
      
      ;; One registry slot per zone id. Small on purpose: a zone holds a full level (hundreds of boxes) in the
      ;; host's own memory, so this is a count of live layouts, not a list of every door in the world.
      (defn zone-max-zones [] : I32 8)
      
      ;; ---- layout parameters ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      ;; A hub plus 2..4 cardinal rooms. 3..5 rooms total, never a diagonal corridor (they are the one case
      ;; that needs corner geometry, and a four-way hub already reads as a dungeon crossing).
      ;; All sizes are world units, matching LevelBox's own convention.
      (defn zone-room-count [(seed : I32)] : I32 (+ 3 (zr-clamp 0 2 (mod seed 3))))
      (defn zone-room-width [(seed : I32) (room : I32)] : I32
        (+ 24 (* 8 (zr-clamp 0 2 (mod (+ seed (* room 37)) 3)))))
      (defn zone-room-depth [(seed : I32) (room : I32)] : I32
        (+ 24 (* 8 (zr-clamp 0 2 (mod (+ seed (* room 53)) 3)))))
      (defn zone-wall-height [(seed : I32)] : I32 (+ 18 (* 6 (zr-clamp 0 2 (mod seed 3)))))
      (defn zone-wall-thickness [] : I32 2)
      (defn zone-door-width [] : I32 8)
      ;; Far enough apart that two 40-unit rooms do not share a wall, close enough that a corridor is short.
      (defn zone-ring-distance [] : I32 52)
      
      ;; Cardinal directions only, 0 = east, 1 = south, 2 = west, 3 = north (x east, z south, matching the
      ;; engine's own yaw-0-faces--Z convention). Room i uses direction (i - 1) mod 4.
      (defn zone-ring-dir-x [(dir : I32)] : I32
        (if (= (zr-clamp 0 3 dir) 0) 1 (if (= (zr-clamp 0 3 dir) 2) -1 0)))
      (defn zone-ring-dir-z [(dir : I32)] : I32
        (if (= (zr-clamp 0 3 dir) 1) 1 (if (= (zr-clamp 0 3 dir) 3) -1 0)))
      
      ;; One spawner in the hub and one per room, so a party never has to walk the whole layout to find where
      ;; it started. Capped at LEVEL_BOXES_MAX_SPAWNERS by the generator.
      (defn zone-spawn-count [(seed : I32)] : I32 (+ 3 (zr-clamp 0 2 (mod seed 3))))
      ;; What the mode's own population should be told to aim for. Twice the rooms plus a little, so a 5-room
      ;; layout is a real fight and a 3-room layout is not empty.
      (defn zone-mob-count [(seed : I32) (rooms : I32)] : I32 (+ (* 2 (zr-clamp 1 8 rooms)) (mod seed 5)))
      
      ;; 0 concrete, 1 metal, 2 brick -- indices into the generator's own material table, which is why this is
      ;; a kind and not a colour: the level file carries the material, the renderer owns the look.
      (defn zone-material-count [] : I32 3)
      (defn zone-material-for [(seed : I32) (idx : I32)] : I32 (mod (+ seed (* idx 7)) 3))
      
      ;; 1..5, the depth of the zone's own dungeon tier -- GFD's state server is what turns this into stats.
      (defn zone-difficulty [(seed : I32)] : I32 (+ 1 (zr-clamp 0 4 (mod seed 5))))
      
      ;; ---- lifecycle -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      ;; Expire only when BOTH are true: nobody is inside AND the grace window has run out. A zone that is
      ;; still occupied never expires, no matter how long the clock says it has existed.
      (defn zone-should-expire [(players : I32) (idle_ms : I32)] : I32
        (if (<= (zr-clamp 0 1000 players) 0)
            (if (>= (zr-clamp 0 2000000000 idle_ms) (* (zone-grace-seconds) 1000)) 1 0)
            0))
      
      (defn zone-elapsed-ms [(now_ms : I32) (since_ms : I32)] : I32
        (if (> now_ms since_ms) (- now_ms since_ms) 0))
      
      ;; 0 uninitialized, 1 active (someone inside or recently inside), 2 idle (empty, counting down).
      (defn zone-zone-status-name [(status : I32)] : I32 (zr-clamp 0 2 status))
