All three landed and pushed as `3a05e0a`.

## Upper floors are populated
Every storey now authors its own zombie, positioned from **that storey's own deck box** rather than the building's overall footprint — without that, the stepped-back buildings (`loft_c`/`d`/`g`) would have put their upper-floor population in mid-air where the lower stack used to be. Result: **61 loft zombies** (2 per ground floor, 1 per floor above, 45 of them upstairs) and **73 authored characters** in the city including the 12 on the bridge.

That needed the character caps to move together again: `LEVEL_BOXES_MAX_CHARACTERS` and `STORY_AI_MAX` went **64 → 128**. The rebuilt `leveltool` confirms it reads all 73 instead of truncating.

## Per-theme loot
Chest tiers belong to the building's theme instead of a 0,1,2 rotation repeated eight times, and they're spread up the building rather than clustered at the entrance:

| theme | tiers | theme | tiers |
|---|---|---|---|
| lab | 2,2,1 | office / cafe / shop | 0,1,1 · 0,0,1 |
| clinic | 1,2,2 | lounge | 1,1,2 |
| workshop | 0,1,2 | warehouse | 0,0,1 |

The built city carries 24 chests across tiers 0/1/2, and `--check` refuses a theme without a loot table or a set of tables too similar to feel different.

## The tree is editable in NOCK
`tools/local_nock.py`'s LevelStore now lists and saves **one directory deep** (`lofts/loft_props_cafe`), `validate_level` accepts a **composition** level (`objects` with `ref_level_id`, quarter-turn `rot_y` only) alongside `walls`, names are slug-checked per segment *and* re-checked for containment after joining, and a new `POST /api/lofts/rebuild` runs the same two commands a human would (`build_loft_city.py` + `update_baked_level.py`) and commits the flattened city and refreshed baked default. The editor gained a **Rebuild lofts → city** button and draws references as dashed anchors with their target ids. It also no longer injects materials/spawner into a composed level on save — that would have rewritten a floor into a different kind of level.

## Checks actually run
- `make test-lofts` — storey-aware population and per-theme loot counts asserted, theme tables distinct, caps, stairs, idempotence.
- `./bin/leveltool check` (rebuilt for the 128 cap) — **1,739 walls, 73 characters**, 1 exit, clean round-trip.
- `make test-local-nock` **16/16** (flat-level and session contracts untouched), `make test-level-save`, `make test-baked-levels`, `make test-witness-ai-zombies` ALL PASS, `make test-empire-spawn` 16/16, `make -B server` links.
- **Live local-NOCK run**: 26 levels listed, 25 in the loft tree; `lofts/loft_pair` shows 0 walls / 2 refs; a composition level saves (200); a props module saves (200); `../x`, `lofts/../x`, `a/b/c` all → **400**; `POST /api/lofts/rebuild` → 200 with the builder's own output.
- Live baked level 92 refreshed to 1,739 walls.

## Named limitations
- **No window**, so a zombie standing on a loft floor has still never been watched pathing — the population is verified as authored data and a clean parse, not as behaviour.
- Upper floors get **one zombie each regardless of floor size**; a 60×20 floor and a 20×60 floor are treated the same.
- NOCK can **see and save** a composed level's references but has no object *placement* tool — adding a reference still means editing the file or the builder's blueprint.

The hang is fixed and pushed (`603ad00`, with a follow-up correction `9c6a5d9`).

## Why it hung
`go build` has **no timeout of its own**, and PITVIPER and IDUNA.GAME are sibling repos whose modules (`go-sdl2`, `x/image`, `x/sys`, `x/crypto`) are **not vendored** in this tree. The Windows OS-apps step called `go build` bare, so a slow or unreachable module proxy parked the job indefinitely — and every artifact behind it waited.

## What changed in `.github/workflows/release.yml`
- **Module cache between runs** — an `actions/cache` step for `~/go/pkg/mod` + `~/.cache/go-build`, keyed on `os_apps/**/go.sum`, so release N+1 doesn't re-download go-sdl2 and friends unless a dependency actually changed.
- **`GOTOOLCHAIN=local`** — Go otherwise decides for itself that it wants a whole toolchain, which is another unbounded download on a pinned runner.
- **A `go_os_app` helper** that bounds `go mod download` at **240s** and the build at **420s**, prints how many `go.sum` entries it's working with, and — if a module still can't be fetched — logs `!! ... module download failed or timed out after 240s -- skipping pitviper.exe`, **skips that one app and lets the release continue**. The lobby's APPS page already reports an unbundled app honestly, and a network hiccup must not hold up the client, server and world that live in this repo.
- The step also no longer fails the job on a missing app: both Go builds are wrapped in `if go_os_app ...; then cp ...; fi`.

## Checks actually run
- `grep` over the whole workflow: **nothing later asserts** `bundled/pitviper.exe` or `bundled/idunagame.exe` exist, so a skip cannot turn into a false release failure (the only `bundled/` assertions are that the *slim* client zips contain none).
- The workflow parses as YAML (PyYAML loads it and finds both new steps), and the **extracted step passes `bash -n`**.

## Named limitations
- **There is no Go toolchain on this machine**, so neither the success nor the failure path of `go_os_app` was executed — I reviewed the skip path (the `if` guard, `timeout ... || exit 1` inside the subshell, the `set -e` interaction) but did not run it. I corrected the CHANGELOG entry to say exactly that rather than claim a test I couldn't perform.
- No Windows cgo SDK here, so a real PITVIPER cross-build wasn't produced either.
- The next real CI run is the proof: expect either all five apps (warm cache, fast) or a clean `!!` line and a release that still ships the C apps.
